prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry in Romanian that build the body, memory and dream into an encyclopedic imaginative cosmos and renew the means of the novel.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: Mircea Cărtărescu (B024) as the single laureate. Nothing in the round-1 exchange has altered my judgment of the works. The case still rests on the common criteria. The voice is recognizable at the level of the sentence and of the whole book. Blinding and Solenoid, as known publicly, are large constructions that rework one imaginative scheme in different forms rather than repeating it. The body, memory and dream function as a cosmology rather than as decoration. I read the oeuvre as mature enough to judge as a whole, with the poetry and shorter prose attached to the same project. The chair asks for a citation that avoids national symbolism, and I have tightened my wording accordingly. It names prose and poetry, since five of six round-1 citations mention poetry in some form. It names Romanian only as the writing language and not as a symbolic claim, and it renews 'the means of the novel' rather than a 'European tradition'. I prefer that to the tradition framing because it describes what the work does and not where it belongs. On the chair's question about late work, I can say only that public reception presents Solenoid as a different construction from the earlier trilogy, which counts against pure repetition. I cannot verify this from the texts. What would count against my case is a Romanian-reading assessment that finds the later volumes recycling the earlier images or sagging over their length. I would then treat the quality as concentrated in a few peaks, which is the test I set in round 1. The unanimous first places in the openings are not evidence for me, and I have not weighed them as such.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that the distinctiveness claim rests on Romanian long-sentence control, rhythm and wordplay, which I cannot assess and which translation may flatten. All six of us are in the same position on this. That makes our agreement weak as corroboration, because we share one blind spot rather than six independent checks. I also cannot rule out unevenness in the longest novels, and the poetry and early work are thinly covered in the translation I know of, so the whole-oeuvre citation is partly an extrapolation from the major novels. Olsson's open question about how an inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing project fits the will's reference to an idealistic tendency is unresolved, and I do not think a single member can settle it. If the committee found that the maximalist scale limits breadth of significance more than it deepens it, Carson (B027) would be the most credible alternative, provided her core oeuvre could be defined as original verse and essay.

responses.point: Olsson, in his case against, leaves open how the will's reference to an idealistic tendency applies to an encyclopedic, inward and often disturbing project like Cărtărescu's, calling it a matter of interpretation. He also keeps Carson as an alternative and reads the public record as showing development in the later volumes.
responses.response: I agree that the will's wording should not be applied before the committee has a shared reading of it. My own reading is that a serious, sustained imaginative engagement with human consciousness, memory and mortality is a defensible way to meet the wording, and that darkness of material is not disqualifying in itself. That is an interpretation, not a settled point, and I would not use it to exclude Carson either. On development I take his reading of the public record as consistent with mine, but we are both relying on reception and not on the originals. So I would not count it as independent confirmation.

responses.point: Mattson names Murnane and Yan Lianke as the strongest alternatives on distinctiveness of voice and formal invention. She says narrowness of range is not a flaw in itself, since intensity is a legitimate literary quality, though she keeps Murnane as an alternative and not as her lead.
responses.response: She is right that intensity is a literary virtue, and I would not penalize Murnane for choosing a narrow field. My hesitation is narrower than that: a body of work built on one deliberate method makes it harder to show significance across the oeuvre as a whole, which is one of the common criteria. His English is also the prose I can approach most directly, so I do not rank him lower for lack of access. I rank him fifth because of breadth. Her round-1 point does make me hold B001 as a live comparison, but it does not move him above Carson or Yan Lianke for me. I would apply the same breadth standard to Murnane, Michon and Wright, as the chair asks.

responses.point: Swärd keeps Yan Lianke (B002) as her first alternative. She argues that his case rests on narrative form and an explicit poetics of mythorealism, with sustained imaginative force across decades and not on political symbolism.
responses.response: I accept that standard and I ranked him third on it. Mythorealism is a real intellectual contribution and not a label. My difficulty is the one the chair's summary records: I cannot judge the Chinese prose register, translation quality varies, and the corpus has been unevenly circulated. I cannot separate his strong books from his weaker ones. That is why I list him as the second alternative, behind Carson, whose core could be defined more cleanly. If Swärd or another member could name the specific titles that carry the sustained-quality claim across decades, that would be useful evidence, but it would need to be more than a restatement of the summary.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Adonis second for reshaping Arabic poetic language. He asks whether the committee has Arabic-language readers who could settle what translation hides, and he declines to give weight to age or timing.
responses.response: I agree that age and timing are not literary criteria. I agree even more with his question about who can read the Arabic. I ranked Adonis fourth because poetry loses most in translation, and I said the same of Cărtărescu's prose. The standard should be symmetrical. If we accept translators' accounts and Romanian-reading assessments as adequate for B024, we should seek Arabic-reading assessments for B035 before judging it. Without them, ranking Adonis lower than a prose candidate is a statement about my access and not about his achievement. For this round I still keep him outside my two alternatives.

responses.point: Palm answers the breadth objection to Cărtărescu by saying his breadth comes from joining the intimate (body, memory, dream) to the encyclopedic and from his reach across poetry and prose. She also holds that Wright's few major novels can still carry sustained achievement if scale and formal reinvention are large.
responses.response: I find her answer on breadth partly persuasive. Breadth by reach across forms is a better argument than breadth by subject matter, and it is the argument I would make. It is still an assertion about the poetry and shorter prose that I cannot demonstrate, because translation coverage there is thin. On Wright I accept that Carpentaria and The Swan Book are very ambitious in language and form, and that a small corpus does not automatically prevent sustained achievement. But I still cannot confirm from public knowledge that her later and nonfiction work deepens them. I rank her sixth and do not move her. If Palm can name what the later work adds, I would reconsider.

uncertainties: My assessment of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose texture, rhythm and long-sentence control rests on public knowledge and translation reception, not on independent reading, and all six round-1 positions share that limitation.
Whether the later very long works deepen the early project or only extend it is read by me from reception, not from the texts. I cannot verify it.
Coverage of the poetry, early work and essays in translation is thinner than for the major novels, so a citation naming prose and poetry is partly an extrapolation.

The application of the will's reference to an idealistic tendency to an inward and often disturbing project, and to ironic or formally radical work such as Carson's, is a matter of interpretation. I have offered a reading but it is not settled.
For Adonis and Yan Lianke I cannot judge the original-language achievement, so the comparison with a prose case I can approach through translation is asymmetrical.
My actual committee voting status as a co-opted member is undocumented, so my simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1, and none apparent that would require recusal. The supplied profile records only institutional connections: election to the Academy in 2020 alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg, work with chair Anders Olsson, and the Permanent Secretary role since 1 June 2026. None of these is a connection to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a non-fiction author and biographer is context, not evidence of a preference for any candidate. I note that the simulated vote reflects a modeling assumption about a co-opted member, and that the conflicts disclosed are not adjudicated here.
